title: Making bee candy for winter feeding
subtitle: A simple hard sugar fondant to place over the cluster in cold months.
excerpt: Bee candy is a firm fondant of white sugar and water, placed directly over the cluster in late autumn and winter to supplement stores when the bees cannot take liquid syrup. The recipe is straightforward: high sugar concentration, a single brief boil, and a cool pour into a shallow tray. It keeps for months at room temperature.
sourceNotes: BBKA Guide to Beekeeping (2nd edn., 2010), winter feeding chapter. National Bee Unit, Feeding Bees Guidance (2022). Dave Cushman, Bee Candy Recipes (archived at dave-cushman.net, public domain).

glossaryTerms.definition: A soft, fine-grained sugar paste used to feed bees when they cannot take liquid syrup. Commercial fondant (bakers' fondant) or home-made candy both work.
A shallow framed board or rim placed above the top super, into which bee candy is poured or placed to allow the cluster to feed from above.

content.text: Bee candy serves a different purpose from autumn syrup. By late October, the cluster is forming and bees will not be moving up through cold air to take liquid feed. Candy is placed directly above the cluster on a
or crown board hole, allowing the bees to access it from below without breaking the cluster.
2 kg white granulated or caster sugar (do not use brown sugar, icing sugar, or sugar with additives)
A heavy-bottomed saucepan and a thermometer that reads to at least 120 C
A flat tray, mould, or candy board frame lined with baking paper to pour into
Combine sugar and water in the stockpot. Stir over medium heat until all sugar is dissolved. Do not allow the mixture to boil before the sugar is fully dissolved, or it will crystallise unevenly.

Once dissolved, increase the heat and bring to the boil without stirring. Clip the thermometer to the side of the pot. Boil the syrup to 116 to 118 C (soft-ball stage). This takes 10 to 15 minutes. Watch it carefully; it rises quickly at this stage.
Remove from heat at 116 to 118 C. Allow to cool to 65 to 70 C, then beat vigorously with a wooden spoon for 3 to 5 minutes until the mixture turns opaque and creamy.
Pour immediately into the prepared tray or frame. The candy sets hard as it cools; a 2 kg batch fills a tray roughly 25 cm x 20 cm x 3 cm deep.
Leave to cool and harden for 2 hours before cutting into blocks if using a tray. Wrapped in cling film, candy keeps for 6 months at room temperature.
Placing the candy on the hive

or candy is placed above the cluster with the exposed surface of the candy facing down toward the bees. Work quickly in cold weather to avoid chilling the cluster. Place the candy directly on the top bars of the highest super, laying it over the feed hole or placing it on a candy board. A block of 400 to 500 g is enough for an emergency top-up; 1 to 1.5 kg is a more typical winter supplement.

attrs.cue: Candy came out crumbly or grainy rather than smooth
attrs.cause: Not beaten for long enough after cooling, or cooled too much before beating
attrs.fix: Beat at 65 to 70 C while the mixture is still hot enough to be mobile. A thin, watery candy beat too early stays liquid; a cold, stiff candy was not beaten in the right window. You can melt down grainy candy and try again.

attrs.cue: Bees are not taking the candy after 2 weeks
attrs.cause: The colony has sufficient stores and does not need supplementary feed, or the candy surface is too hard and dry for bees to access
attrs.fix: Check weight of the hive by hefting (lifting one side). If it feels heavy, the bees do not need the candy yet. To soften the surface, lightly spray the exposed face with water.
